# Individual Discovery

## Overview

This Problem Definition is your first pass at understanding the product opportunity you
may be addressing for the rest of the semester. As an individual, you will use qualitative
and quantitative methods to vet ideas at a high level, evaluating the depth and breadth of
impact a potential product can make for your prospective customers. Everyone will be
expected to share their assessment with the class, which will help facilitate the team
formation and project definition for the rest of the semester.

No solutions at this stage — the bar here is problem clarity. This deliverable covers the
following parts:

- **D1a — Problem Finding & Vetting**
  - D1a-1 — Problem Finding
  - D1a-2 — Problem Vetting
- **D1b — Opportunity Recognition**
  - D1b-1 — JTBD Analysis
  - D1b-2 — Customer Insights
  - D1b-3 — Market Sizing
- **D1c — Pitch the Problem**
  - D1c-1 — The Case
  - D1c-2 — Your Slides

Work the parts in order. The problem you select at the end of D1a is what D1b and D1c run
on, so starting elsewhere generally means redoing work. This is not enforced — you are
welcome to jump around, and nothing is blocked — but your agent will check which problem
you settled on before it helps you with anything downstream.

For how you work with your agent and how to submit, see **How You Work** below.

## Deliverable Instructions

### D1a — Problem Finding & Vetting

One markdown file, `problem-finding.md`, two sections. This is where the deliverable
starts.

#### D1a-1 — Problem Finding

**Objective:** Identify a list of problems worth solving.

**Expected Outcome:** A list of at least 20 problems or unmet market needs.

**Requirements:**
- Create a list of problem areas that you believe can and should be solved by a product.
  Any format is fine — a list, a table, a linked spreadsheet.
- Each problem area only needs to be a one-line description, but should mention the
  prospective customer(s) as well as their needs (motivations and wishes) and/or pain
  points (barriers and current solution deficiencies). For example:
  - Problem area with context: *"Teens and young adults historically do not engage with
    the healthcare system, but can benefit from preventative care and wellness."*
  - Multiple customers with a shared problem area: *"Seniors lack autonomy and
    independence in their healthcare management and decision-making, while giving their
    adult children peace of mind."*
- **NOTE:** It is important and critical for you to stay strictly in the problem space.
  Please do not mention or hint at a solution at this stage — solutioning will happen in
  Unit 2, as a team.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- If you have trouble finding problems, here are two approaches that tend to surface
  different things:
  - *Bottoms-up*… Observe your personal, everyday pain points, including sub-par
    experiences you notice within existing products you would like to correct or
    disrupt. Ask friends and family about annoyances they encounter. Visit a store
    (in-person or online) to find a "stale" category of products that have not undergone
    recent innovation, e.g. hardware stores, toy stores. See Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
    for additional inspiration.
  - *Top-down*… Look at technological (e.g. AI, web3), economic (e.g. inflation,
    evolution of new media), sociocultural (e.g. post-pandemic, rise of Gen Z),
    sociopolitical (e.g. racial equity movement) or any other broad shifts to identify
    emergent gaps and needs. Dive into a community or market (e.g. via forums or
    sub-Reddits) for a given topic or an area of personal meaning to understand that
    community's motivations and frustrations.
- Regardless of which approach you take, some light desk research (e.g. via LLM research
  functions) may be needed to help you understand the problem space.

#### D1a-2 — Problem Vetting

**Objective:** Vet the list and select the top problem to proceed with.

**Expected Outcome:** Each problem vetted and prioritized using a structured framework,
producing the one top problem you will carry through the remainder of this deliverable.

**Requirements:**
- Vet each of the problem areas using some sort of structured framework to identify the
  top problem. For example, create a matrix to qualitatively estimate viability,
  feasibility, and desirability (or any number of criteria) using a "high," "medium," or
  "low" rating, a 1–5 scale, or any other scale you find appropriate.
- Review the results and determine which problem has the greatest opportunity. Proceed
  with the remainder of this deliverable using that problem area.
- If your assessment yields more than one top problem, you may choose one to proceed with
  by perceived likelihood of success, personal interest, project feasibility, largest
  market size, or any other rationale you deem sensible. Please explain your reasoning.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- Problem "desirability" can be assessed across various aspects of needs, like functional
  (e.g. tasks, problems), social (e.g. power, status), and emotional (e.g. happiness,
  security).
- You may find it difficult to assess things like "viability" and "feasibility" without a
  solution in mind, but please be assured that doing so will yield a more objective
  result. For example:
  - For viability, consider strictly your intended customer and their willingness to pay
    for any solution to have the problem solved, rather than focusing on an assumed
    solution.
  - For feasibility, consider the nature and context of the problem. Problems where
    feasibility is inherently low may be problems that are more societal, systemic, or
    physically/scientifically challenging.

### D1b — Opportunity Recognition

One markdown file, `opportunity-brief.md`, three sections. Every section here is about the
problem you selected in D1a-2. This part is the **analysis** — what your research shows.
The **argument** (the problem, whom it is for, why now) is not here; it lives in D1c,
because that structure is what a pitch is made of.

#### D1b-1 — JTBD Analysis

**Objective:** Name the job your customer is hiring a solution to do — not the solution
itself.

**Expected Outcome:** A short paragraph identifying the primary job for the problem you
selected in D1a-2, covering functional / emotional / social dimensions where they
materially change the picture. This is not a checklist to run through all three for its
own sake.

**Requirements:**
- Start from the problem you chose in D1a-2. If that choice has changed, please go back
  and update D1a-2 rather than quietly analyzing a different problem here.
- Cover functional / emotional / social dimensions where they earn it.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- A job is stated as an outcome the customer wants, not a feature they would use. "Get my
  team aligned on priorities without a status meeting" is a job; "a Slack integration" is
  not.
- If you cannot separate the functional dimension from the emotional one, it is usually a
  sign there is more to learn about the problem.

#### D1b-2 — Customer Insights

**Objective:** Conduct an informal interview, then synthesize what it actually revealed.

**Expected Outcome:** An interview of at least 30 minutes, and up to 90 minutes, discussing
the problem with a prospective customer, followed by a short synthesis drawn from the
transcript, with at least one direct quote that carries weight.

**Requirements:**
- **This part starts with an interview.** Conduct it before you write the synthesis —
  there is nothing to synthesize beforehand.
- Your main goal is to learn about the problem space, without diving into what the
  product or solution is yet. Maintain an open-ended conversation.
- Take detailed notes or record a transcript of the conversation, and keep it in your
  repository as supporting material. **The synthesis is written from that real transcript,
  not from memory.**
- Include at least one direct quote, attributed.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- To find an interviewee in your target market, consider sourcing your immediate network
  (e.g. friends, family, former colleagues) or reaching out to relevant groups online
  (e.g. via forum or social media posts).
- Talk to someone who has the problem, rather than someone who will agree with you about
  it.
- A "notable" quote is specific and surprising. If it only restates what you already
  believed going in, keep looking.

#### D1b-3 — Market Sizing

**Objective:** Objectively assess the size of the market for your chosen problem.

**Expected Outcome:** A light TAM/SAM estimate with the assumptions visible, not just the
final numbers.

**Requirements:**
- Show your reasoning: how many potential customers there are, what they would plausibly
  pay, and where those figures came from. A small table with sources is fine.
- You are welcome to use any method of market estimation. Your grade will depend primarily
  on the quality of your assumptions, not the size of the number.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- Your approach may differ depending on your problem space:
  - If this is an existing market, you may start with a pre-determined market size from
    research, inclusive of the expected growth of that market.
  - If this is a brand new, untapped market, your market size will be a function of how
    many total potential customers there are and what their estimated willingness-to-pay
    is for each.
- If you are dealing with a particularly high degree of uncertainty, consider providing a
  market size *range* based on best- and worst-case assumptions rather than a single
  number.
- If the problem is genuinely novel with no comparable market, say so and estimate from
  first principles rather than forcing a comp that does not fit.

### D1c — Pitch the Problem

Drafted in `pitch/outline.md`, with a presentation link in `submission.md`. This is your
s08 pitch. **≤6 slides AND ≤2 minutes total**, including any mixed media; your choice on
the mix. In-class delivery is what influences the vote — and the cohort's vote on the
pitches drives team formation.

#### D1c-1 — The Case

**Objective:** State the problem, **whom** it is for, and **why now** — the argument your
slides will make.

**Expected Outcome:** All three components stated clearly, drawn from your D1b analysis.

**Requirements:**
- Not a formal "problem statement"; just be clear about each component.
- **Do not name a solution.** This is discovery, and a feature list is not an opportunity.
- Draft the content in `pitch/outline.md` — always. This is what is observed.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- "Why now" is a claim, not a formality. If nothing has actually changed, it is worth
  asking yourself why nobody has solved this already.
- If you catch yourself writing "so I'll build…", you have moved past the part being
  assessed.

#### D1c-2 — Your Slides

**Objective:** Deliver the case in ≤6 slides and ≤2 minutes, in whatever medium earns it.

**Expected Outcome:** A deck or recording someone outside your head can follow in two
minutes flat, built for your problem rather than a generic template.

**Requirements:**
- **There is no prescribed slide order, on purpose.** Six slides and two minutes are hard
  caps; what fills them is your call, and choosing well is part of what is assessed. Pick
  what is most compelling *for your problem* — an **intuitive** problem the room already
  recognises needs **quantitative backing** to stay interesting, while a **niche** problem
  nobody has met needs **storytelling** to engender empathy first. Most sit in between.
  Decide where yours sits.
- Build the deck however you like (Google Slides, a deployed reveal.js/Marp deck, or a
  recording) and paste the **link in `submission.md`**.

**Additional Tips & Guidance:**
- Two minutes is not a lot of time. Step back and consider all the factors you have
  compiled throughout this deliverable, prioritizing the data you believe is the most
  compelling. What are the one or two key points your classmates should take away? What is
  the a-ha moment? What qualitative or quantitative data would best make your case?
- If you do not believe your problem area is worth pursuing, please share these thoughts
  with the class. "Failure" is a great teacher.
- Please time yourself before class. Your video or delivery may be cut off at the
  two-minute mark, and there is no penalty for coming in under.

## How You Work

The mechanics: clone/open → commit (with messages) → push → tag. Ask your
agent for the specifics; it handles the details.

- **Author with your coding agent** (Claude Code or Codex). Get started by running
  `/otus-instructions` in your agent within the repo — it walks you through the
  work items above one at a time. Ask it to draft and iterate; your prompts,
  decisions, and revisions are the work. A weak prompt yields a visibly weak
  draft you'll have to improve.
- **Commit as yourself.** Set your own git identity (your name + email) — **not** a
  shared, team, or bot account. Credit is assigned by commit author, so work
  committed under someone else's identity won't count as yours.
- **Wrap each working session** by running **`/otus-session-wrap`** — it commits and
  pushes what you have, records the session's decisions in `notes/session-log.md`, and
  confirms nothing is left unsaved. This is not submission; you can run it as often as
  you like.
- **Record your submission** by running **`/otus-submit`** — it checks the required
  pieces are present, then commits, pushes, and tags `d1-submitted`. See the
  **Submit** task for more details.
